Parametric bootstrap standard errors

Source: R/simulate.R
boot_se.Rd

Simulates R new data sets from a fitted model, refits the model to each, and reports the standard deviation of the refitted estimates. This is an independent check on the standard errors computed from the information matrix.

Usage

boot_se(object, R = 199, seed = NULL, progress = FALSE, ...)

# S3 method for class 'nbzinbreg_boot'
print(x, digits = max(3L, getOption("digits") - 3L), ...)

Arguments

object

An nbreg or zinbreg fit.

R

Number of bootstrap replicates.

seed

NULL, or a whole number for set.seed().

progress

Logical; if TRUE, report progress every 10%.

...

Not used (an error if supplied), except for print().

x

An nbzinbreg_boot object, for print().

digits

Number of significant digits to print.

Value

An object of class nbzinbreg_boot, a list with estimate, se_model (from the information matrix), se_boot (bootstrap), used (replicates used for each parameter), boundary (replicates with that parameter on a boundary), status (counts of the replicate outcomes), failures, boundary_accepted (replicates accepted at the zero-inflation boundary after unconverged refits), R, replicates (the matrix of refitted estimates, NA where left out), notes, and the attribute "seed".

Details

Bootstrap data. A row with prior weight w stands for w independent observations, so w responses are drawn for it independently (a row of weight 0 gets none) and the refit uses the distinct values with their multiplicities as weights. This is exactly the bootstrap of the fully expanded data. Weights that are not whole numbers have no such meaning and are refused. The total number of draws per data set is limited to 1e7.

Safeguarded refits. Each data set is refitted starting from the original estimates. If that refit fails, does not converge, or ends with an estimate on a boundary, the data set is also refitted from the default starting values, and of the refits that converged the one with the higher log-likelihood is used: a boundary estimate reached from one start can be a lower local supremum than an interior maximum reached from another.

The zero-inflation boundary. For zinbreg, a data set may show no zero inflation, so its estimate lies at pi -> 0, where EM can stop unconverged (the zero part drifts toward minus infinity and the interior gradient check becomes unavailable) without anything being wrong. If both refits fail, the data set's negative binomial (NB) model is refitted, and the zero-inflated model is refitted once more from that NB fit with pi near 0. If that refit also fails, the data set is accepted at the boundary only when all of these hold:

  • the zero part has an intercept, so pi -> 0 gives the NB model exactly;

  • the NB refit converged;

  • the score at pi = 0 is not positive, so the likelihood does not rise into the interior;

  • no refit reached a log-likelihood above the NB value by more than 1e-6 (|l| + 1), so no interior improvement was found;

  • the refit from the boundary was monotone and did not fall below the NB value.

The accepted estimate is the boundary point: the count part and theta from the NB refit, with every zero coefficient on the boundary. Otherwise the data set is a numerical failure.

Boundary data sets are kept. A simulated data set can have a maximum likelihood estimate on a boundary: a coefficient running off to infinity, a collapsed zero part (no zero inflation, including a simulated response without any zero), or theta on a bound. These are valid samples, so the data set is kept and only the affected parameters are left out of that replicate. For each parameter, the bootstrap standard error is the standard deviation over the usable replicates in which it has a finite, identified estimate. If more than 5% of the usable replicates put a parameter on a boundary, its bootstrap distribution has mass at infinity or on a bound, and its standard error is reported as NA ("unbounded bootstrap distribution"). Coefficients that already diverge in the original fit get NA too.

Numerical failures are dropped and counted. Up to 10% of R gives an nbzinbreg_warning_bootstrap warning with the counts (dropping them may bias the standard errors downward, if the failed samples are unusual ones). More than 10% gives an nbzinbreg_error_fit.

Parameters. For nbreg: the coefficients and theta. For zinbreg: the count and zero coefficients (named as by coef()) and log(theta). Each zinbreg refit is a full EM fit, so R refits take some time; progress = TRUE reports progress every 10%.

Errors and warnings

  • nbzinbreg_error_input: object of the wrong class, R not a whole number from 2 to 100,000, an invalid seed or progress, non-integer or vanishing frequency weights, a data set of more than 1e7 draws, or unused arguments.

  • nbzinbreg_error_fit: object did not converge (its estimates are not maximum likelihood estimates, so no bootstrap is run), or more than 10% of the replicates failed.

  • nbzinbreg_warning_bootstrap: some replicates failed and were dropped.

See also

simulate.nbreg(), confint.nbreg()

Examples

d <- data.frame(x = 1:8, y = c(1, 0, 6, 1, 9, 2, 20, 4))
fit <- nbreg(y ~ x, data = d)
boot_se(fit, R = 50, seed = 1)
#> 
#> Parametric bootstrap standard errors (50 replicates: 44 ok, 6 with a boundary estimate, 0 failed)
#> 
#>             Estimate Model SE Bootstrap SE Ratio Used
#> (Intercept)  -0.1133   0.8416       1.3149 1.562   49
#> x             0.3440   0.1545       0.2056 1.331   50
#> theta         1.5091   1.0255           NA    NA   45
#> Note: theta: on a boundary in 5 of 50 usable replicates (more than 5%), so the bootstrap distribution is unbounded and no standard error is given.
